newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - unsold cargoes emerge.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - unsold cargoes emerge.

text.p: Supply length has crept into Gulf middle distillates as Asian and Indian subcontinent demand ebbs after recent strong buying, Gulf traders said on Thursday.
Jet kerosene prices and premiums look vulnerable with material unsold from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Bahrain and Indian demand satisfied, traders said.
"The Indonesian buying that we saw last week has disappeared...India only took two kerosene cargoes and there is no support in the market," said one regional trader.
An open arbitrage from NWE/Med to the east has the potential to compete with Gulf middle distillates and light-ends.

The downturn in Asian demand has been felt quickly in Gulf naphtha and jet markets which have fallen 4.6 percent and 1.7 percent respectively in the week. Naphtha was assessed at $191.75 a tonne and jet at $28.55 a barrel fob Gulf on Thursday.
Jet-kero premiums were seen no better than 60-70 cents, but short-term levels would largely depend on Sri Lanka's middle distillate tender which closes Nov 13-15, traders said.

But with refinery maintenance work at Jubail, Saudi arabia and at the Umm al Nar plant in Abu Dhabi planned for November, traders saw limited downside potential during the northern hemisphere's winter.

Gas oil (diesel) has fared better than kerosene markets and has run up a strong premium to jet after being supported by firming Singapore levels which ran back up close to five-year highs on Thursday.
The jet-gas oil spread has moved out to 20 cents in favour of gas oil, compared to jet's 90 cents premium in early October.
Traders' sense that Iraq will not be a factor in the market this year was reinforced by comments made by Iraq's chief oil negotiator Abdul Amir Al-Anbari on Thursday.
Anbari, speaking to Reuters in Geneva, said that he did not expect any change in U.S. attitude to the stalled oil-for-food deal till January at the earliest.
